items.title: Missiles hit Kyiv after Russia agrees to US call to resume Ukraine peace talks
items.summary: Moscow says it is "ready in principle" to resume peace talks and US President Donald Trump says the world is "the closest we've been" to ending the war.
items.content:
Image caption, Russia has in recent weeks intensified its deadly missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities
Ukraine's capital has come under a new missile attack, hours after Russia said it was "ready in principle" to resume peace talks and the US president said the world was "the closest we've been" to ending the war.
Several houses were hit on Wednesday night, injuring six people, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said.
The attack came amid a new diplomatic push led by Donald Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Witkoff met Russia's President Vladimir Putin in the city of St Petersburg on Wednesday - a day after meeting Ukraine's leader.
Three-way talks were paused in February, after which Russia stepped up attacks as Ukraine ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles.
Figure caption, Firefighters tackled blazes across the Ukrainian capital
Speaking on Wednesday, Trump said: "The other day I was talking to Vladimir Putin about settling his war with Ukraine, which I think we're getting closer to, by the way, maybe now the closest we've been."
The US president has so far failed to bring the Russia-Ukraine war to an end despite his repeated comments that he would be able to achieve this.
Rosenberg: US diplomatic push offers little hope for imminent Ukraine peace
Trump's special envoy Witkoff went to St Petersburg after meeting Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky as well as the leaders of Norway and Finland in the Norwegian capital, Oslo, on Tuesday.
It is not clear what specific proposals Witkoff brought to Putin, but Zelensky said after the talks that "strong" security guarantees for Ukraine and energy ceasefire proposals had been discussed.
Putin's aide Yuri Ushakov said their ideas were not very "useful".
Top officials from Russia, Ukraine and the US have held several rounds of talks aimed at ending the war.
Russia blamed last month's "massive" Ukrainian strikes during its general elections for their disruption.
Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.
Image caption, The latest talks between Putin (right) and Witkoff lasted about three hours in St Petersburg
Speaking to reporters after Wednesday's talks in St Petersburg, Ushakov suggested that a new round could be held around 10 November in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates.
He stressed that the talks must focus on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the end of the conflict."
Ushakov also told reporters that Putin reiterated to Witkoff that Russian troops were advancing everywhere across the vast front line and had a "strategic initiative".
Ukraine and its European allies have disputed Putin's claim, pointing to a virtual stalemate on the front.
On Wednesday, Zelensky said he would accept a deal that would freeze the war along the current front line.
"We call it 'ceasefire' or 'stop killings' like President Trump called it. Freeze and stop. And of course this is minimum what we need from Russia today," he told Fox News, adding that security guarantees for Ukraine could be discussed after this.
Figure caption, Watch: Zelensky says US military intelligence sharing "works now"
Witkoff described the latest talks as "constructive", while Kushner, who was participating via a video link, said: "There is still hard work ahead, but we have a real opportunity to move beyond this war and build a framework for lasting peace, security, and prosperity for generations to come."
The talks were held amid a growing row between Ukraine and the US.
Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".
He has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran.
He was also heavily criticised by Democratic and some Republican lawmakers after lifting sanctions on Russia - allowing it to release tonnes of diesel "to the American and global marketplace".
That was despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks earlier.
Zelensky - and Ukraine's European allies - criticised Trump's move.
Last week, Kyiv accused Washington of withholding critical intelligence to warn Ukrainians about incoming Russian ballistic missile launches, resulting in many civilian deaths.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday rejected such accusations as "scandalous", and Zelensky said after the Oslo talks that intelligence sharing "works now" .
Ukraine's military has also complained of speed restrictions to the US satellite internet network Starlink, which constricted its ability to use drones to conduct strikes against Russia.
US officials have denied having requested such a slowdown and a bipartisan group of US senators has called for an urgent investigation .
Image caption, Hubbard had been in jail in Russia for allegedly fighting for Ukraine
Before the Putin-Witkoff talks started, Russia released Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old American citizen who had been given a jail sentence of nearly seven years for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine.
Trump said the former teacher was "on his way back home" and "there was no 'swap' necessary", while Witkoff called Putin a "humanitarian" for agreeing the release.
When asked by a BBC reporter whether he agreed with such a description of the Kremlin leader, US Vice-President JD Vance said: "I agree with Steve Witkoff saying something nice to a person who just released an American hostage.
"Whether you agree with the underlying sentiment or not, Steve Witkoff is a diplomat. His job is to go over there and get a job done. I care much less about what Steve said than about the fact that he is bringing an American hostage home to his family."

Crude oil tankers, bulk carriers and vessels sit anchored near Qaboos Port in Muscat, Oman [File: Elke Scholiers / Getty]
Iran says that seven oil tankers have been struck and sustained damage in the Strait of Hormuz, the largest single-day toll for the waterway since the United States and Israel started their war against Iran on February 28.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said in a statement on Thursday that four of the vessels were transferring oil when they were targeted and caught fire overnight. The other three were disabled after striking mines.

list 3 of 3 Rising costs and tight budgets strain Americans ahead of midterm elections
The claims could not be independently verified, and the report did not provide details about possible casualties or the tankers’ flags.
The IRGC also warned that it could strike US bases across the Middle East if Washington moves to help tankers transit other parts of the strait.
“The US military must know that if this trend continues, the conflict will extend to its bases in the region,” the IRGC said in a statement on its Sepah News website. “This is a serious warning.”
Iran claims control over Hormuz, a strategic shipping route through which one-fifth of the world’s oil supplies passed before war broke out. It regularly attacks ships that attempt to navigate the strait without its authorisation.
But the US military has been escorting vessels through the waterway in increasing numbers, with Iran responding by stepping up attacks.
US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that “Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of oil prior to the US Midterm Election”.
In a post on his Truth Social platform, he added: “They are making up fake hits, mines, and everything else because more oil is coming through the Hormuz Strait now than it did even prior to the beginning of the conflict.”
A US Central Command spokesperson, speaking anonymously to Al Jazeera, also called Iran’s mine claims incorrect.
The spokesperson said US forces have cleared the international shipping lanes of mines and that Iran is using missiles and drones.
The strait remains open, the spokesperson said, with 95 percent of vessels getting through.
The attacks, the spokesperson added, show Tehran’s “desperation” under the US blockade, which cuts Iran off from the resources it needs to rebuild the military capabilities the US has said it destroyed.
“The number of ships and tankers attacked every single day is increasing, and Iran is saying it is continuing to do this because they are not going to allow any change in that situation,” said Al Jazeera’s Mohamed Vall, reporting from Tehran.
“They have full control over the Strait of Hormuz right now, they say.”
Vall said there is also talk in Tehran about an imminent escalation in the war, with the Iranians expecting the US to attack even before US midterm elections in early November.
“The IRGC army chief has boasted that Iran is more ready than anytime before, and has produced enough weapons and equipment to wage a symmetrical war against the United States,” he said.
Reporting from the US White House, Al Jazeera’s Kimberly Halkett said: “Striking Iran does not appear to serve any Republican interests”, adding that pre-election polls tell the same story for Trump’s political party.
“What we’ve seen in surveys in recent months, and as of today, is that most Americans want relief from their tax money going to pay for any potential war with Iran that is ramped up,” Halkett said.
“There is real frustration over the rising cost for everyday Americans, given the rising fuel prices that have occurred as a result of this conflict  … As a result, the US president is having to make the case.
“The pressure is on the president, and it’s not just from the opposition party,” she said. “It is also from within the Republican Party as well.”

WAR IN IRAN, FEDERAL RESERVE RATE HIKE WEIGH ON REAL ESTATE INVESTOR OUTLOOK ACCORDING TO FALL 2026 RCN CAPITAL INVESTOR SENTIMENT SURVEY
WAR IN IRAN, FEDERAL RESERVE RATE HIKE WEIGH ON REAL ESTATE INVESTOR OUTLOOK ACCORDING TO FALL 2026 RCN CAPITAL INVESTOR SENTIMENT SURVEY
Higher Financing Costs, Limited Demand Due to Worsening Affordability  for Homebuyers & Renters Among Factors Keeping Investor Sentiment Weak
SOUTH WINDSOR, Conn. , Oct. 22, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Real estate investor sentiment improved modestly after falling for two consecutive quarters, recovering from an all-time low index score of 84, and improving to 89 in the Fall 2026 RCN Capital/CJ Patrick Company Investor Sentiment Index (ISI)™. The index score marked the third consecutive quarter with a score below 90 and was 12 points lower year-over-year.
Two noteworthy factors appear to be influencing investor sentiment. First, the war in Iran, which nearly 60% of investors feel has had a negative impact on the real estate market. Some 40% cite increased energy costs and rising inflation due to the conflict, which they claim has impacted profitability and reduced demand from prospective homebuyers and renters.
Investors are also nonplussed by the recent action by the Federal Reserve to raise the Fed Funds rate. Over 50% of the respondents agreed that this will make borrowing more expensive, increasing their financing costs and reducing their profitability. There's also a concern that higher interest rates, which have already manifested themselves in mortgage rates climbing to 7.5%, will further hamper affordability for consumers looking to purchase a home, and put more strain on consumer finances for potential renters.
"Investor sentiment has tracked closely with investor activity – industry reports note that investor home purchases in the first two quarters of 2026 were down by 22% from a year ago," said RCN Capital CEO, Jeffrey Tesch. "Hopefully, the improvement in their outlook in our Fall survey is an indication that we'll see investors resume their important role in stabilizing a housing market that's suffering from a dearth of traditional homebuyers."
According to the Fall 2026 RCN Capital Investor Sentiment Survey™, the percentage of investors who viewed today's market as better or much better than it was a year ago, improved from just under 26% in the Summer to 37%, the highest number in three quarters. Those who viewed the market today as being worse fell from 44% to 38%. Similarly, 39% of the investors believe that conditions will improve over the next six months, up from 36% in the previous survey; and the number expecting conditions to worsen held steady at 30%.
"Real estate investors were already dealing with difficult market conditions – relatively high financing costs, limited inventory, rising home prices, and weak demand," said Rick Sharga, CJ Patrick Company CEO. "But the impact of the war in Iran – higher inflation, higher fuel prices, even higher lending costs – has soured investor sentiment, keeping it in line with consumer and builder sentiment, both of which are at or near all-time lows."
Many Investors Finance Purchases, So Lending Costs are Critical Investors responding to this survey mostly finance their property purchases – just under 20% said they made cash purchases – so the high cost of financing continues to be a major headwind. Investors use a variety of loan types to buy properties, including bridge loans, DSCR loans for rental properties, and conventional loans (typically 30-year, fixed-rate loans). Just over half of rental property investors use conventional financing once a tenant is in place.
Unsurprisingly, the high cost of financing continues to be cited as the biggest challenge faced by investors in today's market: over 70% of respondents claimed this was one of the biggest problems today. And almost half of the investors surveyed (45%) don't expect to see relief anytime soon, anticipating that interest rates will stay above 7% between now and the end of the year.
Investor Buying Plans Mostly Status Quo The Fall survey respondents differed a bit from those surveyed in the Summer when it came to their buying plans. About 36% plan to buy between 1-5 properties, down significantly from 55% in the Summer; on the other hand, 26% plan to buy between 6-10, a huge increase from last quarter's 10%; and the percent who plan to buy 11 or more properties doubled, from 3% to 6%. The number of investors who plan to make no purchases in 2026 fell two points, from 32% of respondents to 30%.
For the majority of investors (50%), this is about the same number of properties they purchased in the last 12 months. Only 7% plan to buy more properties than last year, down from 9% last quarter; while about 43% plan to buy fewer, up from 36% in the prior quarter.
In terms of market outlook, the contrast was stark between rental property and fix-and-flip investors. Only 13% of rental investors expected market conditions to get better in this most recent survey, while over 50% expected them to worsen. Flippers' sentiments were almost diametrically opposed, as over 56% of them believed conditions would improve, and just 17% feared that situations would be less favorable in the months ahead.
Insurance Challenges Continue to be a Concern for Real Estate Investors Insurance costs and limited availability of insurance continue to concern real estate investors. Nearly 80% of the respondents said that insurance issues were a factor in their investment decision-making, and 63% said insurance-related factors had caused them to miss out on a deal. Both of these results were more than 10 points higher than in the previous survey.
There were also significant differences between flippers and rental investors in their views on insurance: almost 90% of fix-and-flip investors claim that insurance issues are part of their decision-making process, compared to 69% of rental property investors. And flippers have also lost out on more deals than rental investors, 73% vs. 50%.
Most Investors Expect Home Prices to Rise Despite higher mortgage rates, almost two-thirds of the investors surveyed expect home prices to rise by the end of the year. Over 66% of the respondents said they anticipate higher home prices over the next six months. Almost 43% of the respondents expect those price increases to be higher than 5%, significantly higher than year-to-date price appreciation. On the other end of the spectrum, the number of investors expecting price declines fell by two points, from 13% last quarter to 11%.
Immigration and Tariff Policies Having an Impact Over 48% of the respondents said that immigration policies had made it harder for them to find and keep skilled workers – a 16-point jump from last quarter's results. The number of investors who said immigration policies had increased their construction costs rose from 29% to over 36%. And the number who said that these policies had little or no impact on their investing declined from 50% to just under 38%.
Tariffs also continue to be unpopular among investors: over 62% of investors felt that tariffs had resulted in higher prices on products and materials, up from 48% last quarter; 28% said they'd seen a reduction in their net margins, up two points from the last survey; and 26% said they'd noticed a disruption in supply chains, also rose by six points, from 26% to over 32%. Only 25% of the investors felt that tariffs did not have an impact on their business, down from 30% in the last quarter.
Rising Home Prices, Rising Material Costs, and Limited Inventory Major Challenges
The major challenges cited most often by investors in the Fall survey were similar to those noted in prior reports. But higher interest rates resulted in the number of investors concerned about the high cost of financing to spike, rising from 55% to over 70%. Rising home prices were noted by 38% of respondents, a 10-point dip from the prior quarter. Other frequently mentioned challenges included lack of inventory (31%), and rising material and product costs (23%).

items.content:
Vessels at the strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman. Photograph: Reuters
Vessels at the strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman. Photograph: Reuters
Oil prices jump to five-month high as attacks threaten global supply
Iran’s IRGC says it hit four vessels in the northern Gulf and three more struck mines near the strait of Hormuz
Shipping workers: how is the Middle East conflict affecting you?
Oil prices jumped to a five-month high on Thursday after ​attacks in Saudi Arabia and hits to tankers in the strait of Hormuz threatened further disruptions to the world’s crude supply.
Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, rose by 3% to hit $112 a barrel for first time since 18 May.
Yemeni Houthis , who are aligned with Iran, hit several targets in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, with two people killed and eight more wounded in a civilian airport in Dammam, and two people killed in a drone attack on a Saudi oilfield.
Elsewhere the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said four vessels involved in “illegal” oil transfers in the northern ​Gulf were hit and caught fire after being tracked by its forces on Wednesday.
It said three more vessels collided with mines west of the strait of Hormuz, and warned the US that continued provocations could lead to a wider response against its regional bases.
A chart showing the Brent crude oil price The US has now ordered some diplomats and family members to leave their missions in Saudi Arabia, and it plans to withdraw family members from a number of other missions in the Middle East, according to Reuters, which also reported that Saudi Aramco has instructed staff to evacuate its headquarters in Dhahran and work remotely.
Concern is growing that conflict in the region could escalate further, almost eight months after Tehran’s effective block on the strait of Hormuz triggered what many feared would bring the greatest energy supply disruption in the history of the market. In the first weeks after the US-Israeli attacks on Iran , oil surged past $100 a barrel and market observers predicted prices of up to $150 a barrel as flows through Hormuz came to a halt.
Oil peaked at $126 a barrel in April during the conflict and fell back below $100 in late May and then to lows of $71 at the start of July amid hopes of a ceasefire in the region. The price began to climb again after the memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran fell apart and fresh hostilities broke out in the Gulf .
However, data from Kpler has shown that oil exports from the Persian Gulf have now risen above their prewar levels, partly because of an increase in oil pumped overland through pipelines to the Red Sea and Gulf of Oman.
Global stocks wobbled on Thursday amid expectations of higher inflation and borrowing costs. The Stoxx Europe 600, which tracks the biggest companies on the continent, fell by 1%, with the UK’s FTSE 100 down by 0.7%.
In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei 225 index dropped 2.7%, while the South Korean Kospi fell 3.5%. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng index shed 3%.
Shares in American Airlines dropped almost 4% in pre-market trading after the company warned that high fuel costs would push it into a loss this year.
American Airlines abandoned its previous forecast that it might achieve a profit this year as it faced “historic fuel cost pressure”.

items.title: Rosenberg: Russia agrees to Ukraine talks but sees little to talk about in new peace push
items.summary: President Vladimir Putin does not feel under pressure right now to end the war, the BBC's Russia Editor writes.
items.content:
Image caption, Witkoff (R) said there was still important work to do after the meeting with Putin (L)
By Steve Rosenberg Russia Editor ,Â  Reporting from Moscow
After two days of diplomacy â in Norway's capital and Russia's St Petersburg â is the war in Ukraine any closer to ending?
"Good and constructive" is how Norway's prime minister described Tuesday's talks between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, US President Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and European representatives.
In Oslo, the idea of a trilateral meeting at leaders' level was floated. The hope was that Steve Witkoff's trip to Russia would pave the way for President Vladimir Putin, Zelensky and Trump to meet and agree an end to the fighting.
But Putin has shown little desire to share a table with Zelensky - unless that table is in Moscow.
The Kremlin says it may be willing to resume trilateral talks next month in Abu Dhabi, but only at the technical level.
In a post on X, Steve Witkoff himself conceded that "there is still important work to do", though he claimed "President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end..."
Russia says it is ready to resume talks with Ukraine and US to end war
Trump and Zelensky at loggerheads despite new optimism
US citizen Stephen Hubbard freed by Russia as Trump envoy meets Putin
For me, the most telling statement of the day was from Vladimir Putin's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov. He took part in the St Petersburg talks.
Ushakov said that Steve Witkoff had told President Putin about the discussions in Oslo and (as Witkoff viewed them) "new approaches from the Europeans and Kyiv".
The Kremlin adviser was clearly unimpressed by what he heard.
"In terms of resolving the Ukraine crisis, there wasn't much there that was useful," commented Ushakov.
Later Russian state TV asked him about the prospects for peace.
"I don't know how close we are getting," Yuri Ushakov said, "but things are moving in that direction."
It seems that President Putin doesn't feel under pressure right now to end the war.
He knows that Ukraine's air defences are under severe strain.
He knows that winter is coming and may well view the cold weather as an opportunity to pound Ukraine into submission.
He knows, too, that there is a US president in the White House who clearly wants a bigger, better, more profitable relationship with Moscow.
Image caption, Despite a "constructive" meeting between Witkoff and Zelensky in Oslo, Norway, the idea of a US-Russia-Ukraine trilateral summit does not seem to have taken hold
In recent days Donald Trump has paused some sanctions on Moscow, has agreed to buy Russian diesel and expressed biting criticism of President Zelensky.
That suits Russia just fine. It eases the pressure on the Kremlin leader.
"Right now Trump is the only leader in the Western world who is doing something for peace," Russian MP and TV anchor Evgeny Popov says.
"Doing something for peace, but a peace on your terms?" I respond. "Is that what you want?"
A Putin-Zelensky-Trump trilateral may not be imminent.
But in China next month a meeting between Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping may well take place on the fringes of the Apec summit.
Some commentators here are already dubbing it "The New Yalta" - a reference to the Yalta Conference of 1945, where Stalin, Churchill and Roosevelt met to plan the political and territorial reorganisation of post-war Europe.
"Russia, China and the United States are the only superpowers right now in the world," Evgeny Popov says. "Of course, it will be good for the entire world if our leaders meet in China."
After nearly five years of war, that would put Vladimir Putin exactly where he wants to be - at the top table of global politics.

items.content:
CoreWeave’s market confidence erodes as bond yields spike, stock sinks
CoreWeave's stock is down 35% this month, and the spreads in its credit default swaps are widening.
The company's elevated bond yield is prompting investors to question what additional financing options are available.
"Sentiment is decidedly negative," Andrew Keches, credit analyst at Barclays, wrote in a note to clients this week, referring to AI bonds.
CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator appears after the company's initial public offering at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York on March 28, 2025.
CoreWeave is facing a crisis of confidence on Wall Street that's playing out in real time among equity and bond investors.
With interest rates spiking and AI build-out concerns mounting, debt-heavy neoclouds like CoreWeave are being viewed by many market participants as the most vulnerable trade in the artificial intelligence space.
"Sentiment is decidedly negative," Andrew Keches, a credit analyst at Barclays, wrote in a note to clients on Tuesday, referring broadly to corporate debt in tech. Keches highlighted the "speed at which AI vibes are shifting on a day-to-day basis."
CoreWeave, which went public in March of last year and reached a peak market cap of about $90 billion three months later, is now valued at roughly $31 billion, with its stock down 35% this month after plunging 8% on Thursday. Its unsecured debt, meanwhile, is sporting a yield of about 15%.
The spread on CoreWeave's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, is up 171% in the past year and 36% in October. It last stood at 1,115 basis points, or 11.15%.
The story is playing out across the neocloud sector. Shares of Nebius are down 32% this month, while IREN's stock is down 39%. In Australia, shares of data center operator NextDC plunged 40% on Wednesday after the company slashed its annual earnings forecast. Earlier this month, Australian data center company Firmus scrapped its planned initial public offering, citing market volatility and conditions.
U.K. neocloud Nscale is now under the microscope as investors wait to see whether the Nvidia-backed company will go through with its IPO. The company filed to go public on the New York Stock Exchange last month.
CoreWeave is the biggest of the pack, and is intimately tied to the U.S. AI market. Nvidia is its top institutional investor, with a stake of about 9%, according to FactSet. And more than two-thirds of CoreWeave's revenue last year came from Microsoft .
That's put a spotlight on CoreWeave's financials and its ability to remain viable. The company has about $20.7 billion in debt coming due through 2030 and another $14.9 billion thereafter, with the prospects of higher interest rates on future financing.
Sources on credit desks told CNBC that the high-yield debt market is effectively on hold until after the midterm elections in two weeks given ongoing concerns about the political pushback that data centers are facing. One source, who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the matter, said fixed income investors "want permitting and regulatory requirements to be substantially resolved" before they commit financing.
"Given recent turbulence, pausing makes sense," Seth Meyer, global head of client portfolio management at Janus Henderson, said in an interview.
CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator, who co-founded the company in 2017 initially as a crypto-mining venture, sent a memo to employees on Thursday, which CNBC obtained, to try and tamp down concern. Intrator stressed that the company maintains a range of funding options.
"Our financing model combines infrastructure-backed borrowing, corporate debt, equity, and customer prepayments," Intrator wrote. He added that the company has "additional flexibility to raise equity over time as market conditions and our capital needs warrant."
CoreWeave had $5.5 billion of cash and equivalents at the end of the second quarter. The company is expected to report third-quarter results next month. Analysts expect negative free cash flow in the period to swell to $10.1 billion, the highest since the company started reporting quarterly financials, according to FactSet.
One issue being debated heading into the report is how much more capital CoreWeave needs to raise. Rob Oliver, a software analyst at Baird, is estimating roughly $30 billion in 2027.
"Earnings may address financing measures to shore up confidence," Oliver said in an interview. "But they wouldn't need that capital until the first quarter."
Another question is whether Nvidia will step in if necessary?
Nvidia, which supplies the graphics processing units that CoreWeave rents out, invested $2 billion in January for a 10% stake. The purchase price was $87.20 a share. The stock is now trading at $61.82 even after jumping 6% the day of the announcement.
While Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said last week that CoreWeave doesn't need a backstop, some investors say the chip giant's further participation may be necessary if credit conditions continue to worsen.
Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
Analysts at Goldman Sachs , JPMorgan Chase and Barclays have put out bullish notes on the company this week, highlighting the company's GPU-backed loans and its solid list of investment-grade customers like Microsoft and Meta . Goldman analysts emphasized the company's strength in the market relative to many of its neocloud competitors.
"Not all neoclouds are created equal," they wrote, in upgrading their rating to buy from hold. "CoreWeave is likely in the top quartile of neoclouds, if not the top decile, when measured on performance and ability to execute."
— CNBC's Michelle Fox and Jordan Novet contributed to this report.

Strait of Hormuz Oil Tankers Hit: New Risks for U.S. Farmers
Iran reports seven oil tankers damaged near Hormuz, raising concerns over diesel prices, fertilizer supplies and rising costs for U.S. farmers nationwide.
Marcus Ellington is a U.S.-based journalist covering agricultural markets, global trade, and agricultural policy, with an international perspective on their impact across the global agri-food system.
Iran reported on Thursday, October 22, that seven oil tankers were attacked or damaged by naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz overnight , escalating tensions along a critical global energy route. According to The Associated Press, Iranian state television cited the Revolutionary Guard's navy, although the incidents have not been independently verified. The developments matter to U.S. farmers because disruptions to oil and natural gas shipments could increase diesel prices, fertilizer costs and agricultural transportation expenses , adding pressure to already tight farm margins.
The Iranian account indicated that four tankers caught fire and three others were damaged after reportedly striking naval mines. The British maritime security monitor UKMTO had not confirmed the latest incidents, while shipping operators continued navigating the region under heightened security measures. According to shipping intelligence firm Lloyd's List Intelligence, cited by AP, 28 attacks on commercial vessels have been reported during October , reflecting deteriorating maritime conditions. Despite the threats, oil shipments continue through protected routes, although higher insurance premiums, freight rates and logistical expenses are increasing the cost of moving energy supplies.
Agricultural Biologicals Attract Global Investment as U.S. Innovation and Brazil Drive Growth
Why the Strait of Hormuz Crisis Matters for U.S. Agriculture
The Strait of Hormuz is one of the world's most important oil transportation corridors , connecting Persian Gulf producers with international markets. The U.S. Energy Information Administration estimated that approximately 20.9 million barrels of petroleum liquids passed through the waterway daily during the first half of 2025. Any prolonged disruption could tighten global supplies and increase energy market volatility. For American agriculture, higher crude oil prices can translate into more expensive farm diesel, grain hauling, irrigation and equipment operations , particularly during periods of intensive fieldwork.
Fertilizer markets face another potential source of pressure. Persian Gulf countries are major producers and exporters of nitrogen fertilizers, including urea, while natural gas remains essential to ammonia manufacturing. Higher energy costs and shipping disruptions could increase fertilizer prices for U.S. corn, wheat and other crop producers. Agricultural cooperatives and input suppliers may also face more expensive procurement and transportation. For farmers managing commodity price uncertainty, additional increases in production costs could weaken profitability and complicate purchasing decisions ahead of the next planting season.
Energy markets are already reflecting heightened geopolitical concerns. On October 22, Brent crude climbed toward $112 per barrel , according to market reporting by The Guardian, as attacks and regional instability raised concerns about future supply. However, higher oil prices do not automatically produce equivalent increases in farm input costs. The impact depends on refinery capacity, fertilizer inventories, transportation availability and the duration of disruptions. U.S. producers should monitor diesel quotations, nitrogen fertilizer markets and freight costs , while evaluating purchasing strategies and cash-flow exposure.
For the U.S. agricultural sector, the latest Strait of Hormuz oil tankers crisis highlights how quickly international security threats can affect domestic production economics. Farmers, agribusinesses and agricultural lenders face renewed uncertainty over energy-related input costs , even as global oil shipments continue. Crop insurance and federal farm support programs remain important risk-management tools, but they do not eliminate exposure to rising fuel and fertilizer expenses. The immediate agricultural impact remains uncertain; sustained maritime disruptions would represent a more significant threat to farm profitability and the broader food supply chain.

NEW YORK — Sharp drops for stocks in the AI industry are dragging down markets worldwide on Oct. 22, while oil prices hit their highest levels since May following a report by Iran's state television that seven oil tankers caught fire and were damaged in the Strait of Hormuz.
If the report is verified, it would be the largest number of vessels damaged in the waterway in a single day since the start of the Iran war on Feb. 28..
The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 2.2% to $111.19 after touching its highest level in five months. It's at the high end of the $97 to $112 range it's been yo-yoing through in October on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal.
The S&P 500 sank 0.8% following even sharper losses in Asia, whose markets are full of AI and other technology stocks. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 142 points, or 0.3%, as of 9:35 a.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 1.3% lower.

AI stocks have been shaky on worries that their boom may be under threat because of how expensive it has become to borrow money to build data centers and buy more AI chips. Concerns also remain high that prices simply shot too high for AI-related stocks in their yearslong frenzy, even though companies in the industry continue to report growth.
Lam Research, whose equipment and services help make semiconductors, reported gains in both profit and revenue for the summer that were slightly stronger than analysts expected, for example. Usually, that helps boost a stock's price, but Lam Research's tumbled 10.1% for one of the market's sharpest losses.

It gave a forecasted range for profit in the final three months of 2026 whose midpoint was slightly below analysts' expectations. Its stock also came into the day with a 52.4% surge for the year so far, nearly quadruple the already strong gain for the overall S&P 500, leaving room for potential disappointment.
Other big tech stocks fell following their own profit reports that included at least some encouraging nuggets.
Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, lost 5.7% after reporting stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, though its profit fell short.
Tesla dropped 2.5% despite reporting a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, though its revenue was weaker than forecast .
The global tide against AI stocks knocked Nvidia down 1.8%. Because it's the largest stock on Wall Street by total value, the chip giant was the heaviest single weight on the S&P 500.
CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy Nvidia's AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly shaky in recent weeks because of worries about its debt. It dropped 3.6%, though it's swung between gains and losses of roughly 4% in each of the last two days.
The weakness for AI and other tech stocks began in Asia, where South Korea's Kospi tumbled 3.5%, Hong Kong's Hang Seng dropped 3% and Japan's Nikkei 225 sank 2.7%.

Also weighing on global stock markets was the jump in oil prices.
In Europe, France's CAC 40 stock index fell to one of the continent's sharpest losses with a drop of 1% It has fewer tech stocks than Asian or U.S. indexes, but it was hurt by another jump in yields for French government bonds.
Yields have been generally climbing there because of worries about the government's big debt load and strained budget. Violent protests across France have raised pressure on the government to increase spending, which could add further to its debt.
Worries about big debt affect almost every developed economy in the world, including the United States. Such concerns have pushed yields in the U.S. bond market to their highest levels in decades, along with high inflation , signals of a still-strong U.S. economy and other factors.
But U.S. yields nevertheless fell Oct. 22 in a signal that investors were buying U.S. government bonds in search of something safer to own as AI stocks tumble.
The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 5.05% from 5.13% late Oct. 21 and from more than 5.3% earlier this month. That's a notable move for the bond market, though the 10-year yield remains well above its 3.97% level from before the war with Iran.
The Oct. 22 drop in yields came even as another report suggested the U.S. economy may be doing better than economists expected. It said fewer U.S. workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which could be a signal that layoffs remain low across the country.
That solid economy has helped U.S. companies broadly to make bigger profits, which is what allowed the U.S. stock market to hit its record high earlier this month despite the many worries tugging at it.

CEO Shailesh Jejurikar said Oct. 22 that Procter & Gamble expects "geopolitical and economic challenges" to continue, but it stood by its forecasts for growth in revenue, profit and other measures for the full year. The stock price for the company behind the Crest, Olay and Oral-B brands rose 5.3%.

European Natural Gas Prices Rise on Middle East Escalation
Europe's benchmark natural gas prices rose on Thursday to nearly 90 euros per megawatt-hour, or the equivalent of $29.50 per million British thermal units (MMBtu), as the escalation in the Middle East raised concerns about European winter gas supply amid historically low inventories at the start of the heating season.
The front-month price at the Dutch Title Transfer Facility (TTF) , the benchmark for Europe's gas trading, had jumped by 2.7% at 9 a.m. Amsterdam time on Thursday, tracking a 3% surge in oil prices as the Saudi-Houthi conflict escalates and Iran said it had struck several oil tankers doing transfers in the Persian Gulf.
At $100.84 (89.76 euros) per megawatt-hour (MWh), the European gas price is now at its highest levels since December 2022, when Europe faced the first winter without most of the Russian pipeline gas supply. The current price is also equivalent to about $29.50 per MMBtu.
EU storage sites were only 74% full as of October 21, per data from Gas Infrastructure Europe. That's well below the five-year average of about 86% for this time of the year so close to the start of the heating season.
Prices are vulnerable to further spikes in case of colder winters in either Europe or Asia, or both, or if another supply disruption hits the market.
Early on Thursday, Brent Crude prices hit a five-month high of $112 per barrel, due to fears of further disruptions to supply from the Middle East.
"European natural gas faces similar risks, with relatively low storage levels leaving the region more dependent on continued imports throughout winter," Ole Hansen, Head of Commodity Strategy at Saxo Bank, wrote in a Thursday note .
"A prolonged cold spell, combined with renewed disruptions to LNG shipments, could trigger another sharp increase in prices from the current level around EUR 90 per MWh ≈ USD 29.50 per MMBtu."
As Europe enters the winter with lower-than-usual buffers, and Asia has mostly used its demand-side flexibility, there is a risk of late-winter price spikes, consultancy Timera Energy said last week in its winter gas outlook.
"Our winter 2026/27 outlook assumes Hormuz remains closed through Q4 2026, with gradual reopening through Q1 2027. Under this scenario, late-winter price upside becomes particularly acute if European stocks run low," the analysts said.

items.content:
The United States and Israel are reportedly preparing to resume military strikes on Iran following the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Atta Kenare / AFP via Getty
Oct. 22, 2026, 11:09 AM EDT  /  Updated   Oct. 22, 2026, 2:24 PM EDT
U.S. equity markets sold off sharply Thursday, as fears that Israel and the United States would restart attacks against Iran sent oil prices higher and major tech stocks failed to hold onto recent gains.
The S&P 500 was down 1.3% by 2 p.m. ET, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq had fallen 2.5%. The price of international Brent crude climbed nearly 4%, while U.S. crude gained 2.5%.
Demand for Treasury bonds also increased — bucking the trend of the last several months — as investors sought out the safe-haven assets as riskier ones like tech stocks sold off. That sent the 10-year yield below 5% for the first time since late September.
The market moves were sparked in part by reporting Wednesday that Israel and the U.S. were preparing for a military operation in Iran after the November midterm elections.
Likely targets include Iran’s energy infrastructure and nuclear sites, according to The New York Times.
U.S. military and diplomatic personnel were also being evacuated from several countries in the Middle East on Wednesday, NBC News reported.
Iranian officials have promised widespread retaliation to any strikes, pointing to critical Middle East data center sites and undersea internet cables as potential targets.
“It’s been another difficult 24 hours for markets, as investors grapple with AI growth concerns, higher oil prices, and ongoing fiscal stress,” wrote Henry Allen, director and macro strategist at Deutsche Bank, in a note to clients Thursday.
Major tech stocks led the declines in equity markets, with Meta and Tesla dropping after both companies reported quarterly earnings Wednesday.
Meta, led by Mark Zuckerberg, reported that the expansion of its Muse personal assistant overseas is being hindered by a scarcity of computing power. Annabelle Gordon / Bloomberg via Getty Meta’s earnings and revenues beat forecasts, but only after excluding billions of dollars in legal penalties the company paid last quarter. It also warned investors that it expects to increase its spending in the coming year to meet demands for computing power.
A separate regulatory filing revealed that Meta intends to spend an additional $825 billion on contracts related to its AI infrastructure buildout.
Tesla, meanwhile, said it was reining in its capital spending plans, disappointing investors who were hoping for a signal of more aggressive expansion.
Elon Musk's Tesla reported that it was scaling up its Cybercab fleet in Austin, Texas. Win McNamee / Getty The slide in the Nasdaq got additional fuel Thursday morning after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in an appearance on CNBC that capital to finance the AI investment boom was becoming “scarce” due to higher interest rates and a glut of existing spending commitments.
Despite Thursday’s rout, the S&P 500 remains near the all-time highs it set earlier this month.

items.title: Ukraine war briefing: New peace proposals lack ‘substance’, says Kremlin after Witkoff-Putin meeting in Russia - The Guardian
items.summary: Ukraine war briefing: New peace proposals lack ‘substance’, says Kremlin after Witkoff-Putin meeting in Russia  The Guardian
items.content:
Russian President Vladimir Putin shakes hands with US special envoy Steve Witkoff during a meeting in Saint Petersburg, Russia, 21 October, 2026. Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/Reuters
Russian President Vladimir Putin shakes hands with US special envoy Steve Witkoff during a meeting in Saint Petersburg, Russia, 21 October, 2026. Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/Reuters
Ukraine war briefing: New peace proposals lack ‘substance’, says Kremlin after Witkoff-Putin meeting in Russia
US envoy Witkoff presented Putin with proposals drafted by Zelenskyy and European leaders in Oslo earlier this week. What we know on day 1,702
The Kremlin has criticised new peace proposals to end the war after US envoy Steve Witkoff met with Russian leader Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday. Commenting on the meeting, which followed talks with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European leaders in Norway, the Kremlin warned there was little “substance” in the Ukrainian and European proposals. Despite the lukewarm response from Russia, US president Donald Trump claimed it was “the closest we’ve been” to ending the war. A day before travelling to Russia, Witkoff met Zelenskyy and European leaders in Oslo in a meeting aimed at smoothing over a bitter rift between the Ukrainian president and Trump.
Commenting on the Witkoff-Putin meeting, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters that Russia was “in principle, ready to resume” the trilateral talks in mid-November – after crucial US midterm elections – and that the Kremlin wanted them to focus on postwar security. Ushakov said Witkoff briefed Putin on “some new aspects in the approaches of the Europeans and Kyiv” from the Oslo meeting, but added that “there wasn’t really much substance in them”. Zelenskyy said Kyiv backed resuming trilateral talks as soon as possible.
Witkoff said his talks with Putin were “constructive” but that “there is still important work left to do” . Discussions would continue between the US, Ukraine and Russia at the technical level, he added.
However, the US envoy has face sharp criticism at home for describing Putin as a “humanitarian” , after the Russian leader agreed to free US citizen Stephen Hubbard from a Russian prison. US Republican senator Thom Tillis posted on X: “WTF, Steve? Look up the definition of ‘humanitarian’.” Trump brushed off Witkoff’s comments, saying “I wouldn’t say anything one way or the other”, while US vice-president JD Vance said: “I agree with Steve Witkoff saying something nice to a person who just released an American hostage.”
Later, after a Russian ​strike on ⁠Kyiv that ​followed the talks, Ukrainian foreign minister ⁠Andrii Sybiha said that “appeasement, ⁠servility ​and flattery” ‌would ‌not ‌stop Russia’s war.
Putin’s order to release Hubbard as he met Witkoff appeared to be Moscow’s latest calculated move to bring Trump further into line with Putin’s position on Ukraine while offering the US president a diplomatic victory before the midterm elections, writes Pjotr Sauer . Trump had previously asked Putin to free Hubbard, a 74-year-old former teacher who had spent more than four years in Russian jails on charges of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine. Trump said on social media: “The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return – an unprecedented situation for Russia … There was no ‘swap’ necessary for this release.”
Missiles struck Kyiv in the early hours of ⁠Thursday and Ukraine sent hundreds of drones towards Moscow overnight , authorities said, as the two sides kept up a barrage of attacks ⁠despite the latest ⁠US mediation attempts. The Russian strikes wounded 15 people and damaged subway infrastructure on the Southern Bridge over the Dnipro River in the Ukrainian ⁠capital while also restricting traffic there, Kyiv authorities said. The strikes came after another attack on the city on Wednesday evening that wounded six people. In Ukraine’s north-east, a Russian strike ⁠killed a woman and injured another four people in the Kharkiv region, governor ​Oleh Syniehubov said. And a drone hit energy infrastructure in ‌the Kremenchuk area in the Poltava region, a local official said. In Russia, two people were wounded near Moscow after 630 drones were sent towards the capital during the night, mayor Sergei Sobyanin ‌said. Most of the drones were downed at long range, he added.
US secretary of state Marco Rubio said decisions regarding Ukraine’s access to Starlink were ⁠up to its parent company ⁠SpaceX and Elon Musk, ​not the White House , comments that suggested Musk may have restricted Kyiv’s access to the service. The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Musk had ordered the slowdown of a military-grade ⁠version of Starlink that Ukraine relies on to defend itself against missile attacks from Russia. Meanwhile, Zelenskyy said the US has resumed sharing intelligence with Kyiv about Russian missile strikes after the Norway meeting with Witkoff.

items.title: Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield, and what they mean to Ukraine in the war against Russia - CBS News
items.summary: Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield, and what they mean to Ukraine in the war against Russia  CBS News
items.content:
Over the past week, Ukraine has received a stark reminder of its growing dependence on uninterrupted access to Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield networks in its drone-heavy war against Russia, now in its fifth year.
Ukraine has a fraction of Russia's resources, but its aggressive development of drone warfare on defensive and offensive fronts has helped it endure an onslaught from its much bigger adversary, which invaded Ukraine in early 2022. That was true until last week, when Ukraine reported a throttling of the Starshield network that was causing its drones to stop midflight and fall out of the sky.
The two SpaceX networks operate on a constellation of thousands of low-Earth satellites — Starlink is the commercial version, while Starshield is a military product licensed to the U.S. government and its partners, among them Ukraine.
Kyiv's reliance on drones has made Starlink and Starshield nearly indispensable to its arsenal. When Ukraine experienced a disruption to those networks, it lost the shield of interceptors and drones that offered some protection against Russian drone and missile strikes.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy believes Musk throttled Starshield at the request of U.S. officials , though the world's richest man has denied any role and said it's the U.S. government that controls the military-grade network. President Trump has also denied he's responsible for slowing the network.
However, CBS News reported Tuesday that Musk was behind the disruption, which occurred after he spoke with administration officials multiple times seeking clarity on the president's thinking on the matter, according to sources familiar with the situation.
There has also been conflicting information about whether full access to the networks has been restored. As of Wednesday afternoon, Starlink remained throttled, Zelenskyy's office confirmed.
Here's what's known about Starshield and Starlink — and their role in the Ukraine war.
On Oct. 13, Ukraine's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment, making it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones, officials and soldiers told CBS News .
Ukrainian soldiers said they noticed "speed limits" had been imposed on their use of SpaceX's Starshield internet dishes, the military-grade Starlink dishes that Ukrainians strap onto their drones so remote pilots can maintain their connection with the unmanned aircraft as they fly toward Russian targets.
Access was restricted by turning off dishes on Ukrainian drones flying above a certain speed, causing them to fall out of the sky. Ukraine's Ministry of Defense sources said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions without informing them beforehand.
Zelenskyy said Saturday the speed limits had prevented Ukraine from using Starshield to shoot down Russian Shahed attack drones.
Starshield, the military-grade satellite network, runs on the same constellation of satellites as its civilian sister, Starlink, but has fewer technical limitations and more advanced security features. Both are operated by Musk's company SpaceX.
The U.S. government pays SpaceX to license the use of Starshield and controls who can access the technology. Its use has been limited to Ukraine and occupied territories. It is not available in Russia.
There is no working alternative to Starlink, as no direct competitor approaches Starlink's coverage of 11,150 satellites. Amazon Leo aims to compete, but at this point, it has under 400 satellites in low Earth orbit and has been hampered by the launchpad explosion of a Blue Origin rocket in May.
Regular Starlink terminals have a 70 km/hr (43.5 mph) speed cap, which is the speed at which internet can be used in a vehicle in motion. At rates exceeding the cap, the internet degrades and is no longer usable.
Starshield has no artificial speed cap and is known to work at speeds of at least 160 km/hr (99.4 mph). Starshield-equipped strike drones cruise at 160 km/h or more, and they're the backbone of Ukrainian mid-range strikes.
During the throttling over the last week, Ukrainian units reported link drops at speeds as low as 90 km/hr (55.9 mph), making those drones inoperable. The degradation of Starshield is estimated to have cost Ukraine tens of millions of dollars in losses, according to an analysis by Dimko Zhluktenko, a drone pilot and analyst in the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
On Oct. 15, some Ukrainian officials said that the Starshield restrictions had been lifted. But Zelenskyy told NBC News on Sunday the maximum speed was still 161 km/hr.
Zelenskyy told Fox News on Wednesday that the service was "still limited," but he added that Secretary of State Marco Rubio told him he would "work with his team on this to unblock" it.
Members of a National Police of Ukraine battalion set up a Starlink satellite communication terminal at a combat position in the Donetsk region of Ukraine on Oct. 16, 2026.
Photo by Dmytro Smolienko/Ukrinform/NurPhoto via AP
It uses both. Starlink has been providing internet service to Ukrainian civilians and military forces since 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, according to Reuters .
Initially funded by private donors and a U.S. foreign aid contract, SpaceX won a Pentagon contract to pay for Starlink for Ukraine in 2023, along with a contract for 500 Starshield terminals.
In August 2024, SpaceX signed another Defense Department contract to expand Starshield usage to 3,000 terminals for the front lines, Bloomberg reported.
Beyond communicating with and guiding drones over long distances, Starshield also serves another function: It connects every sensor and weapon system on the battlefield. Disruptions to the service have an impact that can be compared to an office having to function without being able to connect to Wi-Fi.
Ukraine's military uses Starlink for general battlefield communications, and Ukrainian civilians rely on it for communications needs, too.
On the Russian side, the Kremlin had also been using Starlink until February, when SpaceX cut off its access. As a result, Ukraine gained more than 150 square miles of territory.
CBS News reported Tuesday that a decision by Musk led to restrictions on Ukraine's use of SpaceX's satellite communications network, though it remains unclear how Musk's order to curtail service was executed.
Musk had spoken with administration officials multiple times, seeking clarity on the president's thinking on the matter, sources said. He has in the past expressed distaste for the perception that his company could be seen as profiting from the Ukraine war.
The temporary restrictions came as a surprise to some Trump administration officials, who said neither Mr. Trump nor the Pentagon had specifically ordered any limits meant to deliberately disrupt drone operations and battlefield communications.
The president said Monday he was seeking information about who had ordered the slowdown. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday denied the Pentagon had manipulated the service, saying, "We haven't made any directives or anything like that."
Can Elon Musk stop the use of Starlink and Starshield?
Musk has not admitted to imposing restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starshield.
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," the world's richest person wrote on X .
He added that Starlink is a "commercial service," writing that it is "limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action."
Rubio, however, seemed to attribute the network constraints to Musk.
"The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr. Musk," Rubio told reporters in Mumbai on Wednesday.
Within a few minutes, though, he seemed to concede that Starshield was different: "We don't control what a private company — how they decide their product can be used. Now, if they're in a contract with the United States military, like Starshield, that's a different matter, because that's something we are purchasing and using for our use."
At around the same time as the Starlink and Starshield disruptions, Ukraine also did not receive warnings from U.S. intelligence about major Russian strikes.
Ukraine relies on a mixture of American sensors, aircraft, surveillance and human intelligence to map Russian positions and launch sites.
The early warning system, which is distinct from the SpaceX products, notifies Ukraine when Russia has launched a ballistic missile in its direction. It failed in at least two instances, on Oct. 13 and Oct. 18.
On Oct. 13, Zelenskyy said Ukraine "received no advance warning" when Russia launched a ballistic missile barrage. That overnight attack targeted energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv and Kharkiv, killing six people and leaving some 600,000 without power.
Ukrainian sources said U.S. officials said the warning system had failed due to "bad weather." Ukrainian officials expressed doubt about that explanation and accused the U.S. of "playing" with the system. By 3 a.m., that system seemed to have been restored.
Then on Monday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had been hit by another wave of Russian missile and drone strikes, "and again, there was no warning from partners."
A senior Pentagon official told CBS News Monday there had been "no change to Department of War policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities we are enabling Europeans to provide to Ukraine."
By Wednesday, however, the warning system appeared to have been restored: "Now intelligence works. Thank you so much. That was crucial for us," Zelenskyy said on Fox News.
Deliveries of key Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine have also slowed, Ukraine has said.
Rubio on Tuesday called interceptors the "most in-demand product right now in the defense field," and said that "when a country doesn't get interceptors from the United States, it's not because we're denying. We have our own needs, too."
"There's nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine," he said. "It's simply a balance between our obligations."
Mr. Trump has grown impatient with the more than four-year-long war. He has sought to portray the ongoing Ukraine war as the reason for high energy prices and has vented his frustration with Zelenskyy more frequently in recent weeks, accusing him of not doing enough to end it.
He waived restrictions on buying Russian diesel earlier this month in an effort to ease pressure on the price of the commodity, a move Zelenskyy argued could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin. And Mr. Trump also waived sanctions on Russia last week.
Mr. Trump said earlier this month that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop striking each other's energy infrastructure — announcing an "energy ceasefire." Zelenskyy initially said Ukraine was willing to abide by such an agreement, but that Russia's strikes never ceased, and several days later he told the Financial Times his country would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries because Russia was still attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
The Russian government never confirmed that it had agreed to a ceasefire.
Mr. Trump told reporters Tuesday that Russia keeps "grinding away" and is more capable of sustaining casualties than Ukraine, arguing "it's time" for Zelenskyy to make a deal.

items.title: The Latest Inflation Data Spells Bad News for Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and the Stock Market - The Motley Fool
items.summary: The Latest Inflation Data Spells Bad News for Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and the Stock Market  The Motley Fool
items.content:
The U.S. Federal Reserve is tasked with keeping inflation under control, which typically means targeting an annual increase of around 2% in the Consumer Price Index (CPI). When inflation is too high, it puts pressure on household budgets and reduces corporate profit margins, so the Fed often hikes the federal funds rate (overnight interest rates) to put the brakes on the economy and cool prices down.
The CPI rose at an annualized rate of 3.4% in August, prompting the Fed to hike rates for the first time in three years at its September meeting. Fed chairman Kevin Warsh also warned more rate increases might be on the way if inflation remains persistently high, and the latest batch of data suggests that is exactly what is happening.
Rising interest rates can spell bad news for the stock market for a few reasons. In fact, the Fed's last rate-hiking cycle resulted in a bear-market decline of over 20% in the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC -1.43% ) index. Here's what investors need to know.
The U.S. and Iran have been locked in a fierce geopolitical conflict since late February. In an attempt to gain leverage, Iran has closed the Strait of Hormuz waterway, through which 25% of the world's seaborne oil transits each day. To make matters worse, the ongoing conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen took a turn for the worse recently, knocking even more oil supply offline.
As a result, a single barrel of West Texas Intermediate crude trades for over $100 as I write this (Oct. 19), a whopping 77% increase from its 2026 opening price of $57. Consumers now face soaring prices at the pump, but they are also paying more for groceries and retail products because it's suddenly more expensive to fuel the trucks, boats, and planes used to transport them.
The CPI increased at an accelerated annualized rate of 3.7% in September, with the energy component jumping by 20.4%. But it could get worse, because the September Producer Price Index (PPI) increased by 6.3%, with energy surging by 35.4%. The PPI measures the change in input costs for businesses, which are typically passed on to consumers through higher prices, so it's often a leading indicator of future CPI readings.
The CME Group 's FedWatch tool, which tracks the probability of interest rate moves by analyzing the 30-day Fed Funds Futures market, suggests there is a 91% chance of another 25 basis-point hike in December. It also predicts two more hikes in March and June 2027, so it seems Wall Street is betting that high inflation is here to stay.
Rising interest rates are bad news for the stock market
When interest rates rise, consumers are forced to allocate more of their household budgets to debt repayments, leaving less money for discretionary spending. Over a long enough period of time, this can put a dent in corporate earnings, and earnings typically drive stock prices.
High interest rates also make companies think twice about borrowing money to fund their expansion plans, so investors start pricing in slower sales and earnings growth, which often leads to lower stock prices. Better yields on risk-free alternatives like cash and government Treasury bonds only accelerates the shift away from stocks when the growth outlook is uncertain.
The Fed's last rate-hiking cycle spanned from March 2022 to August 2023, and the S&P 500 was down more than 20% at its lowest point during that period, officially placing it in a bear market .
It's impossible to predict how long the Fed's current hiking cycle will last, but the S&P 500 is especially vulnerable to a correction right now because of its valuation. It's trading at a Shiller Cyclically Adjusted Price-to-Earnings (CAPE) ratio of 41, the second-highest level behind only the peak of the dot-com bubble in the year 2000. In fact, the index's CAPE ratio is so high that it might still be expensive even after a bear-market decline of 20%.
As a result, investors should tread with caution right now, particularly if they are trading risky derivatives like options contracts, or using margin loans to amplify their returns. These practices can lead to substantial losses if volatility ramps up.
The best approach is to stay focused on the long term. History suggests the market tends to recover and set new highs given enough time, so using a potential dip to buy an S&P 500 index fund and consistently adding to the position could yield excellent results over a period of 10 years or more.

North Korea prepares to restart propaganda loudspeakers as ties sour with South
Kim Yo-jong, sister of Kim Jong-un, issues warning after inspecting border fortifications against backdrop of rising tensions
Propaganda loudspeakers aimed at South Korea will be ready to restart within days along the entire border, Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, has said amid a worsening of ties between the two countries.
The statement, carried by the state news agency KCNA on Thursday, came a day after she said the loudspeakers would be in operation along the whole border from some time in October.
Both North and South Korea have historically used giant loudspeakers to broadcast propaganda across the border, with the North in recent years playing haunting bestial howls, and the South opting for K-pop music ​and news criticising Pyongyang.
If the broadcasts resume, they would be the first loudspeaker exchange across the border in 16 months. South Korean president Lee Jae Myung suspended broadcasts from the southern side just days into his presidency in June 2025 to ease tensions with Pyongyang, and the military dismantled the speakers that August.
At a briefing on Thursday, a defence ministry spokesperson in Seoul said that if North Korea went ahead, “naturally there would have to be a proportional measure”, but made clear no decision had been made.
A North Korean military guard post featuring loudspeakers, seen in February 2026. Photograph: Ahn Young-joon/AP The joint chiefs of staff said routine maintenance of the North’s loudspeakers had been observed before Kim Yo-jong’s statements.
Tensions between the two Koreas have risen since September, when a landmine blast south of the military demarcation line injured three South Korean soldiers, two of them seriously.
Seoul and the UN command – which oversees the 1953 armistice that halted but did not end the Korean war – concluded it was a North Korean anti-personnel mine and an armistice violation. Pyongyang denied responsibility and called the incident a “self-staged farce”.
The loudspeaker threat comes as North Korea continues to fortify its side of the border. Since Kim Jong-un declared that the two Koreas were “two states hostile to each other” in December 2023, North Korea has laid mines, strung barbed wire and erected anti-tank barriers along the border.
On Wednesday, Kim Yo-jong inspected several fortification points along the border with Pak Jong-chon, a marshal and adviser to Pyongyang’s defence ministry.
The border had been “clearly blocked and turned into a fortress more thoroughly”, she said, adding that Kim Jong-un had told her it “should be a permanent line never to be crossed”.
Seoul says North Korean troops have repeatedly crossed the military demarcation line, the 250km line dividing the two Koreas, during the construction work, prompting South Korean soldiers to issue warnings over loudspeakers and fire warning shots.
North Korea has called the warning shots and broadcasts provocations by “armed rogues”.

Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq tumble as oil climbs, investors weigh Meta, Tesla earnings
Updated Thu, October 22, 2026 at 1:07 p.m. CDT 1 min read
US stocks fell on Thursday, led by the Tech ( XLK ) sector as the AI trade unwound and Wall Street assessed earnings from EV maker Tesla ( TSLA ) and social media giant ( META ). Investors flocked to bonds, sending Treasury yields lower as oil prices surged to a five-month high .
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) declined 0.3%, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) fell 1.5%. The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) tumbled 2.7% as semicondcutor stocks fell, reversing gains from Wednesday's session.
Meta shares tanked as investors weighed the company's quarterly results and 2-for-1 stock split announcement.
Tesla shares were volatile after an earnings beat , as investors weighed lower 2026 capex against higher spending in 2027 and 2028 on Optimus, Cybercab, and Terafab. SpaceX ( SPCX ) stock fell, giving back more than half of Wednesday's post-earnings gain.
Meanwhile, Blackstone's ( BX ) stock climbed 6% following the firm's upbeat outlook for upcoming investment sales after posting weaker third quarter earnings amid elevated borrowing costs.
A report that the US and Israel are preparing for renewed attacks on Iran after the US mid-term elections sent Brent crude ( BZ=F ) to $113 per barrel while West Texas Intermediate crude ( CL=F ) climbed to $100. A deadly attack at a Saudi Arabian airport and oil field also put upward pressure on energy prices.
In other news, jobless claims fell to 194,000 last week , the fewest in three months, underscoring how layoffs remain low.
Meta stock drops more than 6% despite strong Q3 results, stock split
Bitcoin ( BTC ) fell below $82,000 early Thursday as crypto joined a broader sell-off in riskier assets amid rising geopolitical tensions.
The world's largest cryptocurrency traded around $81,600 Thursday morning, down more than 3% for the last 24 hours. Other major coins also declined.
Crypto's total market value fell 1.4% over the previous 24 hours, according to CoinMarketCap. Traders saw roughly $400 million in liquidations over the same period, according to data aggregator CoinGlass.
If oil is about to spark an inflation wave, the bond market hasn't heard about it.
The 10-year Treasury yield (^TNX) is on track for its biggest one-day drop in more than two years on Thursday, slipping back below 5% as stocks slide. The 5-year yield (^FVX) is falling even faster. Meanwhile, Brent crude (BZ=F) is hovering around $112, up more than 50% since the Iran war began in late February.
The surprise is how little the oil spike has moved the bond market's inflation forecasts.
The 5-year breakeven — the inflation rate implied by the gap between regular Treasurys and inflation-protected TIPS — is a bit lower now than it was before the war.
The 5y5y inflation swap is the market's forecast for average inflation over the five years starting five years from now, and the Fed watches it closely for signs that expectations are slipping. It has barely moved.
So the jump in yields since February has been almost all about real rates — not inflation. Traders are betting the Fed keeps policy tight enough that $110-plus oil doesn't turn into lasting inflation.
Not everyone buys it. Bloomberg strategist Simon White argues breakevens are "mispricing" the oil shock.
Elsewhere in bondland, France's 10-year yield is above the US 10-year for the first time since 2013.
Next up is the 5-year TIPS auction at 1 p.m. ET. Bloomberg's Alyce Andres calls it a referendum on the Fed's inflation bet under Chair Kevin Warsh. Weak demand would signal investors are starting to doubt it.
Bitcoin falls below $82,000 as investors retreat from risk assets
Bitcoin ( BTC ) fell below $82,000 early Thursday as crypto joined a broader sell-off in riskier assets amid rising geopolitical tensions.
The world's largest cryptocurrency traded around $81,600 Thursday morning, down more than 3% for the last 24 hours. Other major coins also declined.
Crypto's total market value fell 1.4% over the previous 24 hours, according to CoinMarketCap. Traders saw roughly $400 million in liquidations over the same period, according to data aggregator CoinGlass.
Treasury yields retreat as AI trade comes under pressure, investors flock to bonds
Treasury yields fell as investors flocked to bonds amid pressure on the AI trade.
The 10-year Treasury yield ( ^TNX ), which moves inversely to bond prices, fell 11 basis points to 5.02%. The 30-year Treasury ( ^TYX ) yield also slid 10 basis points to 5.32%.
Concerns over a slowdown in AI infrastructure build-outs overshadowed inflation fears stemming from higher oil prices.
Blackstone stock climbs 4% as executives give upbeat Q4 exit outlook
Blackstone (BX) stock rose 4% Thursday morning, reversing earlier losses as executives at the alternative asset giant offered an upbeat outlook for investment exits and fee growth in the coming quarters.
Blackstone CFO Michael Chae told analysts that performance-fee realizations from investments already under contract and expected to close in the fourth quarter would surpass the firm's total net realizations in the third quarter. He also reiterated expectations for "double-digit" growth in base management fees in 2027.
The outlook offered investors some encouragement after Blackstone reported a 34% drop in net realizations during the third quarter compared with a year earlier while distributable earnings fell 9% in the same period.
CEO Stephen Schwarzman described the quarterly results as "strong" amid a "volatile external environment" in a statement accompanying the earnings release.
US stocks fell as investors digested earnings from Meta and Tesla while oil prices and government bond yields remained elevated.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) declined 0.3%, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) dropped 0.9%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) tumbled 1.4%.
Shares of Meta ( META ) and Tesla ( TSLA ) each fell more than 3% at Thursday's open while Oil prices also rose while the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield ( ^TNX ) hovered around 5%.
Chip bulls sprang a bear trap on Tuesday. Two sessions later, they're the ones getting caught.
The iShares Semiconductor ETF ( SOXX ) is down about 4% premarket, below Tuesday's intraday low of $489.70. That was the floor of the bear trap — a breakdown that quickly reverses, catching traders betting on further losses. SOXX is on track for its lowest close since July 29.
Lam Research ( LRCX ) is leading the slide, down about 9% after its results Wednesday night. Applied Materials ( AMAT ) and KLA ( KLAC ) are off about 6%, and AMD ( AMD ), Intel ( INTC ), and Sandisk ( SNDK ) are down 4% to 5%. Nvidia ( NVDA ) is off a milder 2%.
SOXX is on track to flip direction for a fifth straight session, and the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) for a seventh.
Dip buyers keep showing up anyway. Semiconductor ETFs saw record flows over the past week, Bloomberg senior ETF analyst Eric Balchunas posted Thursday. "Buying the dip here has [a] pretty good record of working," he wrote.
There's little room to hide. "Every index on the planet is basically an AI index," Manulife John Hancock Investments co-chief investment strategist Matt Miskin said on Yahoo Finance's live show Thursday.
Watch whether buyers come in yet again this session. A close above $490, roughly Tuesday's trap low, keeps the bulls' hopes alive — barely.
Oil prices rise to highest level since May on worries of Iran-US escalations after midterms
Oil prices rose on Thursday to their highest level since May amid growing worries over an escalation of the war in the Middle East after the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Brent crude ( BZ=F ) topped $111 per barrel, while West Texas Intermediate crude ( CL=F ) hovered above $98 a barrel.
The US and Israel have reportedly drawn up plans for renewed attacks on Iran after the elections next month, according to the New York Times , citing unnamed US officials.
Meanwhile, Middle East tensions escalated after Saudi Arabia said it suffered attacks at the airport of Dammam and an Aramco oil field .
Tesla reports Q3 earnings beat, positive free cash flow, and better-than-expected capex
Tesla ( TSLA ) reported better-than-expected third quarter earnings on Wednesday, with its free cash flow and capex spending coming in ahead of Wall Street estimates.
Tesla reported Q3 revenue of $28.05 billion vs. Bloomberg consensus of $28.13 billion. Tesla posted adjusted EPS of $0.48 vs. the $0.44 estimate, with adjusted EBITDA of $3.90 billion vs. $3.66 billion.
Tesla stock was volatile following the earnings release.
IBM shares slide as revenue outlook holds steady despite earnings beat
IBM ( IBM ) shares were volatile in pre-market trading on Thursday after the company beat Wall Street's top- and bottom-line estimates and raised its full-year free cash flow forecast, but maintained its 4%-5% revenue growth guidance for 2026.
Software revenue accelerated by 9%, but CFO Jim Kavanaugh said about a quarter of that growth came from closing "tens of slip deals" that were delayed from the second quarter.
This suggests third-quarter software growth was partly driven by delayed revenue rather than entirely by new demand.
